# 34 Extent of Lymphadenectomy for Esophageal Cancer

title: "Extent of Lymphadenectomy for Esophageal Cancer"

## Introduction: The Controversy
    
- **The Debate:** Does radical lymph node dissection provide improved locoregional control and survival?
- **Disease Nature:** Aggressive; local nodal and distant metastases often exist at presentation.
- **Neoadjuvant Therapy:** Frequently used for locally advanced disease intended for potential cure.
- **Staging Benefit:** Extended lymphadenectomy improves staging, allowing better patient counseling and guiding adjuvant treatment.

## Lymphatic Drainage & Embryology
- **Anatomy:** Esophagus traverses three body compartments with wide spread patterns.
- **Embryology:** 
  - *Above:* Branchial arches and pharyngeal pouches.
  - *Below:* Splanchnic mesoderm.
- **Demarcation:** Tracheal bifurcation leads to bilateral lymphatic drainage.
- *(Reference: **Fig 34.1** illustrates the bidirectional lymph flow from the esophagus based on this embryological demarcation).*

## Patterns of Spread: Early Cancer
- **Anatomical Pathways:** Tumor location dictates likely nodal involvement.
  - **Above tracheal bifurcation:** Upper mediastinum and neck.
  - **Below tracheal bifurcation:** Toward the celiac axis.
  - **At bifurcation:** Can metastasize in either direction.
- **Skip Metastases:** Skipping of lymph node stations in early tumors is **rare**.

## Patterns of Spread: Advanced Cancer
- **Submucosal Network:** Extensive longitudinal communication between proximal and distal systems.
- **Eccentric Involvement:** Occurs when primary pathways are blocked by advanced tumors.
- **Clinical Reality:** Most patients present at advanced stages.
- **T3 Disease:** Associated with up to an **85% chance** of lymph node involvement.

## Early Node Involvement: SCC vs. Adenocarcinoma
- When tumor invades the muscularis mucosa (T1a-M3):
  - **Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC):** Up to **12%** lymph node involvement.
  - **Adenocarcinoma:** Only **1.3%** lymph node involvement.
- Highlights the differing early biological behaviors of the two histologies.

## Lymph Node Tiers: The "Fields"
- Dissection is commonly divided into three anatomical fields:
  1. **Upper Abdomen**
  2. **Mediastinum**
  3. **Neck**
- **Three-field dissection:** Removal of nodal tissue from all three areas.
- *(Reference: **Fig 34.2** maps the extent of resection and fields routinely carried out for esophageal cancer).*

## Defining "Two-Field" Dissection
- Definitions vary by regional pathology prevalence:
- **East (SCC prevalent):** 
  - Upper abdomen (celiac) + inferior/superior mediastinum + recurrent laryngeal nerves.
- **West (Adenocarcinoma prevalent):** 
  - Upper abdomen + inferior mediastinum (usually extending only to the carina, reflecting lower esophagus/EGJ tumor locations).

## 1st Field: Abdominal Lymph Node Dissection
- **Superior Gastric Group:** Paracardial (left & right), lesser curve, and left gastric artery nodes.
- **Celiac Trunk Nodes:** Root of left gastric, common hepatic, and splenic arteries (removed *en bloc*).
- **Common Hepatic Nodes.**
- *Note:* Disease beyond celiac/hepatic drainage equates to **metastatic disease**.
- Intramural spread to abdominal nodes is greater in Adenocarcinoma (54%) vs. SCC (10%).

## 2nd Field: Thoracic Lymph Node Dissection
- **Standard Mediastinal:** Pulmonary hilar, paraesophageal, carina, bronchi, and paratracheal nodes (taken *en bloc* with esophagus).
- **Extended Mediastinal:** Adds nodes on the right side of the trachea.
- **Total Mediastinal:** Additional removal of nodes along the left recurrent laryngeal nerve and subaortic nodes.

## 3rd Field: Cervical Node Dissection
- **Target Nodes:** Brachiocephalic, deep internal, and external cervical nodes.
- **Recurrent Laryngeal Nerves:** Includes left and right RLN nodes.
- **Involvement Frequency:** Deep external (lateral to IJV) and deep internal (approx. RLN) are more commonly involved than deep lateral (spinal accessory chain) nodes in thoracic carcinomas.

## Box 34.1: Nodes According to Anatomic Region

| Anatomic Region | Lymph Node Stations |
|---|---|
| **Cervical** | Deep lateral, Deep external, Deep internal |
| **Superior Mediastinal** | Recurrent nerve chain, Paratracheal, Brachiocephalic, Infraaortic-arch |
| **Middle Mediastinal** | Tracheal bifurcation, Pulmonary hilar, Paraesophageal |
| **Lower Mediastinal** | Paraesophageal, Diaphragmatic |
| **Superior Gastric** | Paracardial, Lesser curve, Left gastric artery |
| **Celiac & Hepatic** | Celiac trunk nodes, Common hepatic nodes |

## Depth of Invasion & Nodal Involvement
- **Confined to Mucosa:** 0%–7% for both SCC and Adenocarcinoma *(supports endoscopic resection)*.
- **Submucosa Invasion:**
  - **SCC:** Up to 50%
  - **Adeno:** 15%–50%
- **Transmural / Muscularis Propria:**
  - **SCC:** >73%
  - **Adeno:** Up to 80%

## Recurrence Patterns
- **SCC (Law et al.):** 2/3 recurrences in 1st year. Majority extrathoracic (distant organs > lymph nodes). Local recurrence ~25%.
- **Adenocarcinoma:** Local recurrence ~9% (lower esophagus) to 15% (junctional).
- **Overall:** Local recurrence for either subtype is **25%–50%**, indicating meticulous lymphadenectomy profoundly impacts locoregional control.

## Mapping Junctional Cancers (Kurokawa et al.)
- **Category 1 (>10% involvement, Strongly Recommended):** Abdominal stations 1, 2, 3, 7, 9, 11p. Lower mediastinal (110) if >2cm esophageal involvement.
- **Category 2 (5-10%, Weakly Recommended):** Abdominal 8a, 19, lower mediastinal 110.
- **Category 3 (<5%, Not Recommended).**
- *Finding:* Even with 4cm esophageal involvement, no mediastinal nodes reached Category 1.

## Fig 34.4: LN Metastases in Adenocarcinoma

*(Visualizes predominantly downward lymphatic spread based on extracted figure data)*


- **Data Points:** 50.6% | 43.9% | 31.5% | 12.8% | 10.2% | 9.7% | 5.4%
- **Takeaway:** High incidence in abdominal and lower mediastinal nodes; cervical involvement is relatively low, supporting 2-field dissection for typical lower/EGJ tumors.

## Implications: Rationale for Extensive Dissection
- **Locoregional Control:** Leaving positive nodes behind equates to leaving disease behind.
- **Staging Accuracy:** Prevents stage migration and guides adjuvant therapy.
- **Resection Margins:** Complete resection (R0) is vital. Microscopic (R1) or macroscopic (R2) residual disease yields a significantly bleaker prognosis.

## Prognosis & Node Location
- Location of nodal involvement is an independent predictor of survival (Anderegg et al., Adenocarcinoma):
  - **Locoregional nodes only:** 35 months survival
  - **Celiac trunk nodes:** 16 months survival
  - **Proximal field nodes:** 15 months survival
- Trend toward greater 5-year survival with extended *en bloc* transthoracic vs. transhiatal approaches (Hulscher et al.).

## Lymph Node Yield vs. Survival
- **Conflicting Data:** Some studies (Van der Schaaf, Lagergren) found higher yields didn't equate to better survival *(Note: upper quartile yields were low at 15-20 nodes)*.
- **Meta-Analysis (Visser):** Higher lymph node yield **is** associated with improved survival in both neoadjuvant-naive and treated cohorts.
- **Optimum Thresholds:** 
  - **23 nodes** (Peyre et al.)
  - **31 to 42 nodes** for T3+ disease (Rizk et al.)

## Lymph Node Ratio (LNR)
- Ratio of positive to negative nodes is often a better prognostic predictor than the "N" category alone.
- **SCC (Chen et al.):** "Nr" categories (0, 1-10%, 10-20%, >20%) predict survivals of 61%, 41%, 33%, and 23%.
- **Adenocarcinoma (Bhamidipati et al.):** Confirmed LNR as an independent predictor.
- **Caveat:** LNR is useless if insufficient nodes are obtained (incomplete sampling).

## Micrometastases & Tailoring Dissection
- **Micrometastases:** Present in up to 50% of N0 patients; explains node-negative recurrences. Prognostic impact remains debated.
- **Tailoring:** Ideally, dissection would be tailored to disease stage.
- **Sentinel Nodes:** Unreliable due to skip metastases and unpredictable nodal involvement.
- **Extended Resection:** Most beneficial in patients with **<8 lymph node metastases** (Omloo et al.).

## Predicting Systemic Disease (Peyre et al.)
- Can systemic disease be predicted by the number of involved nodes?
  - **> 3 nodes involved:** Probability of systemic disease exceeds **50%**.
  - **> 8 nodes involved:** Probability approaches **100%**.
- Suggests a threshold where extensive surgery may no longer confer a survival advantage due to the systemic nature of the disease.

## The Three-Field Lymphadenectomy Debate
- **Japan:** Widely employed. SCC is prevalent, and almost **33%** of patients have cervical node involvement.
- **The West:** Infrequent. Driven by concerns over morbidity and the extrapolation that cervical node involvement equates to systemic (M1) disease with no survival advantage.

## Three-Field Outcomes (Lerut et al.)
- Evaluated mixed cohort (pre-neoadjuvant era).
- **Cervical Node Involvement:** 25% of patients (75% undetected on initial staging).
- **5-Year Survival with Positive Cervical Nodes:**
  - EGJ Adenocarcinoma: 0%
  - Distal-third Adeno: 12% *(4-year was 36% $\rightarrow$ palliative role?)*
  - Middle-third SCC: **28%**
- **Conclusion:** Cervical nodes shouldn't always be deemed "metastatic", especially in SCC. Complication rates were not significantly higher.

## Cervical Node Involvement in SCC (Chen et al.)
- **Proximal third tumors:** 44% cervical involvement.
- **Lower third tumors:** Strikingly, **23%** still had cervical node involvement.
- Systematic reviews in predominantly SCC populations demonstrate **superior survival** with 3-field dissection.
- **Adenocarcinoma:** Routine cervical dissection is generally not merited unless extensive mediastinal nodal disease is present.

## Morbidity of Extended Lymphadenectomy
- **Respiratory:** Pneumonia, ARDS. Impaired lymphatic flow compounds pulmonary edema from one-lung ventilation.
- **Direct Injury Risks:** Tracheobronchial tree, Recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN palsy), Thoracic duct (chyle leak).
- **Quality of Life:** Swedish nationwide study found **no association** between the number of lymph nodes removed and QoL at 6 months or 5 years post-surgery.

## High Volume Centers & Robotic Approaches
- **High Volume Units (Henckens et al.):** High lymph node yields are achievable without increasing complication rates. Yields >31 nodes improved survival.
- **Robot-Assisted (RAMIE):** 
  - 50% suffered major complications (RLN palsy, pneumonia).
  - Only 5% had unexpected contralateral LN metastasis.
  - *Takeaway:* High morbidity exists for potentially little oncological benefit if extensive dissection is not properly indicated.

## Summary & Current Guidelines
- **AJCC 8th Edition (2018):** Groups N category by the *number* of positive nodes but fails to specify an adequate yield, risking understaging.
- **Morbidity:** Several studies refute the claim that comprehensive lymphadenectomy inherently causes unacceptable morbidity.
- **Adjuvant Therapy:** Adequate staging identifies candidates for adjuvant treatment, improving 1- to 5-year survival.
- **Distinct Entities:** Future studies must treat SCC and Adenocarcinoma as distinct entities with different behaviors.

## Conclusion & Surgical Advocacy
- Leaving positive nodes behind is likely to hasten recurrence.
- While neoadjuvant treatments may sterilize remaining disease in some patients, this impact is **impossible to predict**.
- **Authors' Advocacy:** Unequivocally advocate an **en bloc lymphadenectomy** (complete two-field minimum) in all patients where nodal involvement is a concern.
- Decisions for 3-field dissection should be dictated by extent of disease, likelihood of recurrence, histology, and overall fitness in a multidisciplinary setting.
